questions.q: When your shell runs a command like 'ls', how is the new process actually created on Linux?
choices: The kernel builds a brand-new process from scratch for the program.
The shell forks a copy of itself, then the copy calls exec to replace its program with ls.
The shell asks systemd (PID 1) to spawn ls directly.
exec creates a new process and fork loads the program into it.
questions.explain: A new process is never made from nothing. The shell calls fork() to clone itself, then the child calls exec() to overwrite its memory with ls — keeping the same PID and open files. That FD-preserving step is exactly why shell redirection works.

questions.q: You spot several zombie (defunct) processes in 'ps'. What is actually going on, and what fixes it?
choices: They are using lots of memory; kill -9 each one to free it.
They are orphans the kernel forgot; reboot to clear them.
They have exited but their parent hasn't reaped them; you can't kill a zombie, so fix or kill the parent.
They are stuck in uninterruptible sleep; wait for their disk I/O to finish.
questions.explain: A zombie has already exited — it holds no memory and runs no code, just a PID and exit code waiting to be collected. You can't kill something that's already dead, so kill -9 does nothing. The real culprit is a parent that isn't reaping, so you fix or kill the parent and PID 1 cleans up.

questions.q: A process's parent dies while the process is still running. What happens to it?
choices: It becomes a zombie and must be killed manually.
It is immediately terminated by the kernel.
It is re-parented to PID 1, which will reap it — this is normal and harmless.
It keeps the dead parent's PPID until it exits on its own.
questions.explain: This is an orphan, not a zombie. The kernel re-parents it to PID 1 (systemd), which dutifully reaps it when it finishes. Orphans are routine; zombies are the pathology. The two are often confused but are essentially opposites.

questions.q: Why is 'kill -9' (SIGKILL) considered a brutal last resort rather than the normal way to stop a process?
choices: It is slower than SIGTERM because the kernel has to confirm it twice.
It can't be caught, so the process gets no chance to flush data, release locks, or reap children — risking corruption and zombies.
It only works on processes you started yourself, unlike SIGTERM.
It always leaves the process running if it is in the background.
questions.explain: SIGKILL is uncatchable, so the process runs no cleanup at all — buffers aren't flushed, locks aren't released, children aren't reaped. Send SIGTERM first (plain 'kill PID') to let it shut down gracefully, and escalate to -9 only if it ignores you. SIGKILL isn't even all-powerful: a process in uninterruptible (D) sleep won't die until its I/O completes.

questions.q: You start a long job over SSH and want it to keep running after you log out. How do plain '&', 'nohup', and 'disown' differ?
choices: All three do the same thing; the names are just aliases.
'&' alone reliably survives logout; nohup and disown are only for redirecting output.
nohup makes the process ignore SIGHUP before launch; disown removes the job from the shell's table after launch; plain '&' does neither robustly.
disown changes the signal before launch and nohup changes the shell's bookkeeping after launch.
questions.explain: They solve overlapping problems by different mechanisms. nohup sets the process to ignore SIGHUP before it starts (and redirects output to nohup.out); disown changes the shell's own job bookkeeping after the job is running so it won't be sent SIGHUP on exit; plain '&' just backgrounds the job and does neither robustly. For real detachment, tmux/screen or a systemd service is the modern answer.
